entries.title: Munetaka Murakami goes 1-for-3 with two strikeouts in first rehab game
entries.summary: <p>White Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami went 1-for-3 with a single and two strikeouts while playing five innings at first base Tuesday in his first rehab game at Triple-A Charlotte. There’s no set timeline for his return, but it’s plausible that he’s in the Sox’ lineup Friday for the opener of a series against the Athletics.</p><p>“There’s a game plan to build him up throughout the week,” Sox manager Will Venable said. “Take it day by day to see how he’s feeling and recovering and see if he’s getting enough at-bats. And then hopefully at some point before the break, we’ll activate.”</p><p>Venable has said he expects Murakami, who strained his right hamstring May 29, to play a couple of games in Charlotte. If that’s the case, Murakami could play Wednesday and travel Thursday to Chicago.</p><p>His return will necessitate a difficult roster decision. Jacob Gonzalez is playing well at first base and coming on at the plate. But there might not be playing time available elsewhere on the infield, where he actually has more experience.</p><p>“Every one of these guys has contributed,” Venable said. “We’ve been talking about that in every one of these wins, every one of these games. That makes it tough when you have guys that you’re bringing back and getting healthy because everyone has done such a good job. Good problems to have, but we’ll figure it out when we get there.”</p><h3>Injury updates</h3><p>With rain pouring and the field covered before the game Sunday in Cleveland, injured Sox outfielder Austin Hays ran sprints in right field under the supervision of trainer Brad Lawson. Hays is on the 60-day injured list with a strained left calf.</p><p>“He looked really good running, and so he’ll continue to run and take [batting practice], and then we’ll see how it goes over the All-Star break relative to being able to move around,” Venable said. “And then if he’s in a good spot, we’ll look at what a rehab assignment would look like.”</p><p>Outfielder Everson Pereira still is battling symptoms from a concussion. Venable described him as day-to-day.</p><p>“Still working through getting the intensity up with the activities without having symptoms,” he said.</p><h3>Oh, Noah</h3><p>Left-hander Noah Schultz had another rough outing in his second start since returning from the injured list (tendinitis in right knee). In five innings, he allowed four runs, seven hits (two home runs) and three walks with three strikeouts. In 10 starts this season, he has a 6.00 ERA (32 earned runs in 48 innings).</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Years marveling at this version of Pete Crow-Armstrong? ‘It’d be pretty special’ for Cubs
entries.summary: <p>BALTIMORE — Cubs center fielder <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong </b>had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/02/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-player-of-the-month-june-stats-babe-ruth-lou-gehrig-shohei-ohtani" target="_blank" >a June for the ages</a>.</p><p>His next trick? Well, it’s not slowing down.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong is off to the races in July, starting the month 8-for-17 in five games, including two hits and an RBI in the Cubs’ 5-2 victory Tuesday against the Orioles.</p><p>After batting .381 last month, he’s off to a .471 beginning to this month.</p><p>Yeah, yeah, small sample size. Still, the guy’s on fire.</p><p>‘‘Obviously,’’ Cubs president <b>Jed Hoyer </b>said toward the end of June, ‘‘he’s not going to play like this the whole season.’’</p><p>Are we sure about that?</p><p>Crow-Armstrong’s teammates are still marveling, awestruck by the transformation the 24-year-old has made. He reached base at a .287 clip and walked only 29 times in 157 games last season. He has a .383 on-base percentage and has walked 41 times in his first 91 games this season.</p><p>‘‘The most impressive thing is the plate discipline and the walks,’’ outfielder <b>Ian Happ </b>said. ‘‘For him to get to this point this quickly and really, in a matter of a week or two, kind of change the way that he approaches at-bats and the patience, the ability to lay off some really tough pitches . . . that’s been the most impressive thing to watch. [It’s] just the consistency of the quality of at-bats.</p><p>‘‘There’s always been thump there. There’s always been unbelievable tools and the speed and the defense. What he did last year was so special. But . . . to watch the way that he’s walking, it makes him so lethal because he’s such a good baserunner.’’</p><p>And there’s a whole lot of career left for Crow-Armstrong, a long-term franchise cornerstone, thanks to the contract extension he signed before the season that runs through 2032.</p><p>Isn’t it worth wondering whether the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/04/pete-crow-armstrong-lone-cubs-all-star" target="_blank" >the newly minted two-time All-Star</a> can reach even greater heights? Or, given that his month of June <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/03/pete-crow-armstrong-had-a-june-that-compares-with-babe-ruth-and-lou-gehrig" target="_blank" >put him in the same club</a> as <b>Babe Ruth</b>, is that asking too much?</p><p>‘‘If you bottled this player that he is right this second and gave him 15 more years of that, it’d be pretty special,’’ Happ said. ‘‘There’s always room to get better at things, but this version of him in the last month is pretty spectacular.’’</p><h3>Boyd, Bregman best Birds</h3><p>Left-hander <b>Matthew Boyd </b>and third baseman <b>Alex Bregman </b>helped the Cubs to their victory against the Orioles.</p><p>Boyd, who could <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/01/cubs-matthew-boyd-all-star-ace-starting-rotation-pitching-injuries-craig-counsell-pete-crow-armstrong-alex-bregman-thumbs-down" target="_blank" >help buoy the Cubs’ banged-up pitching staf</a>, was stellar in six scoreless innings, looking like his normal self after a couple of starts coming off the injured list.</p><p>‘‘He was amazing,’’ catcher <b>Miguel Amaya </b>said. ‘‘He was dialed in from Pitch 1. He dominated the zone, and the other team, they had no chance against him.’’</p><p>Meanwhile, Bregman, a player with a big contract and a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/05/the-cubs-alex-bregman-is-showing-signs-of-heating-up" target="_blank" >big bat that’s starting to emerge</a>, had two hits and two RBI.</p><p>Momentum — just in time for the All-Star break.</p><p>‘‘I was talking to [Orioles slugger <b>Pete</b>] <b>Alonso </b>about that at first base,’’ Bregman said with a chuckle. ‘‘He was like, ‘You feeling better?’ I was like, ‘Yeah.’ He was like, ‘Yeah, and in five days, you get the All-Star break.’ I was like, ‘Perfect.’ ’’</p><h3>Time for Taillon?</h3><p>Right-hander <b>Jameson Taillon </b>still might <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/30/cubs-jameson-taillon-hamstring-injury-return-injured-list-pitching-injuries-starting-rotation-drew-pomeranz-minor-league-deal" target="_blank" >return from the injured list before the All-Star break</a>, but the Cubs hope they don’t have to bring him back that quickly.</p><p>Manager <b>Craig Counsell </b>said the team is planning for Taillon to follow his minor-league rehab start Sunday with another. But should a need arise during the Cubs’ road trip, they could bring Taillon back sooner for what Counsell called a ‘‘limited’’ outing.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module entries.title: Man fatally shot in North Lawndale alley
entries.summary: <p>A man was found fatally shot Tuesday morning in North Lawndale, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Howaun Roberts, 20, was in an alleyway in the 3400 block of West Polk Street at 9:56 a.m. when he was shot multiple times, according to police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>He was taken to Illinois Masonic Hospital where he later died, police said in a statement. No arrests were reported.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man fatally shot on Near North Side
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot early Tuesday on the Near North Side, Chicago police said.</p><p>Javanti Smith, 40, was outside in the 400 block of West Evergreen Avenue around 2:10 a.m. when he was shot multiple times, police said. </p><p>The man was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where he was pronounced dead, police said. His name was released Tuesday evening by the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>Area detectives were investigating. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man found fatally shot in Back of the Yards
entries.summary: <p>A man was found fatally shot in Back of the Yards Tuesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 26, was found with a chest wound near the street in the 900 block of West 54th Street at 6:50 p.m., police said. He was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center and pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>Police reported no arrests.</p>

entries.title: Sky's Skylar Diggins and coach Tyler Marsh still not aligned after benching
entries.summary: <p>PHOENIX — On Day Two of the “Abruptly Benching a Future Hall of Famer” chapter of the Sky’s season, Tyler Marsh and Skylar Diggins still are not on the same page.</p><p>Marsh reiterated Tuesday that his conversations with Diggins would stay private. Diggins said they had not spoken further about the decision and then sat out the game with a right knee injury.</p><p>“It just seems like a basketball decision,” Diggins told the Sun-Times. “When I came here, I was told I was going to hold it down until Slooty [Courtney Vandersloot] got back, so I still don’t have very much clarity on that. If it was something different outside of that, I have to defer to him.”</p><p>She added: “I don’t know if it was because Sloot is available now and that’s how he envisioned it.”</p><p>Looking back, Diggins said she is not sure what “holding it down” until Vandersloot returned really meant.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/06/skylar-diggins-caught-off-guard-by-benching-as-tension-builds-with-sky" >Skylar Diggins caught off guard by benching as tension builds with Sky</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Vandersloot has returned from an ACL injury and immediately reinvigorated the offense, even on a minutes restriction. Natasha Cloud also moved into the starting lineup against the Mercury, sending rookie Gabriela Jaquez to the bench.</p><p>One can point to plenty of legitimate basketball reasons to move Diggins to the second unit. Her defense has been inconsistent. Her efficiency at the rim has declined.</p><p>Marsh gave a vague explanation for the lineup change on Tuesday.</p><p>“It’s been a little of [our slow starts], and a little of some other stuff, chemistry-wise and whatnot,” Marsh said of the change to the rotation.</p><p>Heavy emphasis on the “chemistry-wise and whatnot.”</p><p>If this were only about basketball, it should not be so hard to explain publicly or privately.</p><p>We want more size. We want more rebounding. Pick your reason.</p><p>Cloud and Jacy Sheldon both have rotated out of the starting lineup this season with basic basketball explanations.</p><p>Diggins said Tuesday that Marsh did not necessarily owe her one.</p><p>But the Sky signed Diggins to a fairly expensive two-year deal. They lauded the move as proof their franchise was turning the corner. They have spent all season downplaying concerns about the wisdom of building around three highly accomplished veteran point guards.</p><p>Some sort of explanation — public, private or preferably both — will eventually be necessary.</p><p><b>Getting what you signed up for</b></p><p>Signing Diggins, a seven-time All-Star, this offseason was supposed to show that things were going to be different in Chicago.</p><p>It helped push back on the narratives surrounding the franchise and its ability to attract and retain star players.</p><p>Marsh even leaned into that idea during Diggins’ introductory news conference, saying she had been around the league long enough to discern “the fake from the real.”</p><p>The Sky had been handpicked by a future Hall of Famer. A star who wanted to bring her toughness and credibility to their young core. </p><p>A player who, they also had to know, had a reputation for speaking her mind and sometimes creating friction.</p><p>She publicly called out the Mercury organization in 2023 after she said she was not allowed to use their facilities during maternity leave. She got into it with then-teammate Diana Taurasi on the bench in 2022 and then missed the rest of the season, including the playoffs.</p><p>The full Diggins experience has followed her to Chicago — the accountability, the bluntness, the public call-outs and the emotion.</p><p>Diggins went public Monday, saying that the experience in Chicago has not matched what she expected, citing miscommunication from staff and a lack of resources.</p><p>She can be a handful during games — yelling at staff, sometimes arriving late to midgame huddles or missing them altogether.</p><p>Amid all of that, she has had real leadership moments. When she called out the team during its losing streak, Cloud said it lit a fire under them. Cloud also has talked about Diggins providing useful messages during the losing stretch, like remembering that basketball is a “get to,” not a “got to.”</p><p>In other words: The Sky are getting the player they signed, in the situation they signed her into.</p><p>They signed a star who does not pull punches, placed her in a crowded backcourt with two other veteran guards who also needed heavy minutes and paired all of that with a second-year coach still learning the finer points of team management.</p><p><b>The late-game disconnect</b></p><p>There is no one reason for the Sky’s 6-14 start. Not Diggins, not Marsh. But closing out games is one of them.</p><p>The Sky are 3-8 in clutch games, ranking 14th out of 15 teams.</p><p>Asked why the Sky have struggled to close games, Diggins said she wanted to choose her words carefully to avoid being a jerk.</p><p>“We don’t discuss late game very often,” she said. “I don’t think we have a set/reset play to run. We’ve been in that situation a lot of times. I would love to hear what [Marsh’s] late-game strategy is as far as what exactly we’ve been doing. It’s something we didn’t really work on a lot in preseason. We’ve found ourselves in certain predicaments over and over again. I don’t really know what the adjustments are.”</p><p>Still, Diggins took accountability for herself.</p><p>“From my player perspective, it’s mistakes that we’ve made as players that put us in that predicament,” she said. “But we take our cues in those situations from our coach. He’s the boss. He makes all the decisions.”</p><p>And the picture is genuinely mixed. Diggins is always in the closing group. She is the Sky’s second-highest clutch scorer behind Sydney Taylor. But her efficiency in those moments is just 31.6%.</p><p>Marsh, has taken accountability, too, but did not have a grand analysis on Tuesday.</p><p>“We just have to close games out,” Marsh said. “We’ve put ourselves in position of being in tight games. We’ve been in situations where we’ve been able to extend games. There’s been a couple of breakdowns here and there. Overall, we’ve been prepared in those moments. We’ve just come out on the short end at times.”</p><p>He believes they have been prepared. She would love to hear the plan.</p><p>The good news, though, is that Diggins does think the Sky are playing a better brand of basketball overall.</p><p>“What I mean by that is showing resistance, not getting first quarter lulls, not falling to double-digit deficits in the first half,” she said.</p><p>Marsh has been saying that, too. entries.title: Attorneys general, state officials sue over 2nd federal attempt to cut permanent housing funds
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul, along with officials from 20 states and Washington D.C., are suing the Trump administration following its second attempt to restrict funding for homelessness housing support.</p><p>On June 1, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development tried for a second time to limit money for Continuum of Care-funded permanent housing programs. The move included shifting $1.3 billion in funding for permanent housing programs to those for temporary housing.</p><p>Raoul and the coalition of state legal officials said the move, which they argue oversteps the Trump administration’s power and violates federal law, will once again risk housing for tens of thousands of people. In Illinois alone, $60 million in funding would be lost, according to the suit.</p><p></p><p>The Department of Housing and Urban Development didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p></p><p>In November 2025, the Trump administration <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/12/03/chicago-homelessness-trump-housing-policies" target="_blank" ><u>proposed sweeping cuts</u></a> to grant funds for permanent supportive housing to the tune of $3.9 billion, including eliminating money for any organization recognizing the existence of transgender people and removing groups that provide services for people with mental health-related disabilities.</p><p>A coalition of more than a dozen state officials, which also included Raoul, sued in the wake of those funding changes, saying it would have put 170,000 people at risk of losing housing. In Illinois, they say it would have impacted housing for 7,500 people as $182 million in funding was threatened.</p><p>That coalition of state officials won their lawsuit to keep the funding when a federal judge ruled on June 30 that the administration had overstepped in trying to control the funding allotted by Congress.</p><p>Similar arguments made by Raoul and others have led to federal court decisions reinstating <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/24/illinois-wins-suit-on-disaster-relief-funding-held-by-dhs-over-sanctuary-laws" target="_blank" ><u>$2 billion in federal disaster relief funding</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/11/04/judge-blocks-trump-administration-transportation-funds" target="_blank" ><u>$2 billion for transportation</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/06/appeals-court-kwame-raoul-trump-administration-medical-research" target="_blank" ><u>millions in public health research money</u></a>. Another federal court decision halted a Trump administration <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/22/federal-trade-commission-world-professional-association-transgender-health" target="_blank" ><u>attempt to restrict federal funds</u></a> to any healthcare institution providing gender affirming care to patients under 19-years-old.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/08/29/chicago-housing-groups-brace-for-possible-sweeps-of-homeless-encampments-by-national-guard" >Chicago on guard for sweeps of homeless encampments</a> new policies on homelessness criticized</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The more than 1,300 people <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/01/21/more-than-58-000-chicagoans-experienced-homelessness-new-report-says" >in Chicago without housing on any given day</a> have been frequent Trump administration targets.</p><p>Last summer, President Donald Trump signed an executive order<a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/ending-crime-and-disorder-on-americas-streets/" target="_blank" ><u></u></a> that <a class="Link" to remove outdoor homeless encampments and forcefully institutionalize people if they wanted the funds. Advocates and care providers have said the order <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/07/26/trump-order-targets-homelessness-visibility-not-solutions-advocates-say" target="_blank" ><u>targets homelessness visibility, not solutions</u></a>.</p><p>Months later, city residents braced for the potential of National Guard troops descending on the city and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/08/29/chicago-housing-groups-brace-for-possible-sweeps-of-homeless-encampments-by-national-guard" target="_blank" ><u>clearing homeless encampments</u></a> as they had in Washington D.C., though the troops never deployed to Chicago.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/01/22/officials-volunteers-conduct-census-of-chicagoans-experiencing-homelessness-as-dangerous-wind-chills-arrive" >Census of homeless Chicagoans taken amid biting wind chills</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/05/20/latinos-homeless-chicago-illinois-greg-abbott-texas-busing-migrants" >More Latinos are homeless in Illinois, spurred by Texas busing migrants to Chicago, report finds</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/30/chicago-heat-wave-extreme-weather-brandon-johnson-health-south-side-west-side" >As temperatures soar, city urged to add nighttime cooling options for vulnerable residents</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: White Sox reliever Seranthony Dominguez having 'a hard moment'
entries.summary: <p>When the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" > White Sox</a> signed Seranthony Dominguez in January, they anticipated him closing a lot of games for them. They didn’t give him a two-year, $20 million contract for mop-up duty.</p><p>Dominguez expected to be the closer, too. But more than three months into his deal, he not only isn’t closing, he isn’t pitching in high-leverage, late-game situations. He’s tied for second in the major leagues with five blown saves, and his 4.85 ERA would be the worst of his career.</p><p>“It’s a hard moment for me right now,” Dominguez told the Sun-Times before the Sox’ game Tuesday against the Red Sox. “I’m trying to do my best. I didn’t get the start that I’m looking for. But I’m still trying to find a way to help the team win. Doing my best, put on my best face, [giving] my best effort every time I go out.”</p><p>The Sox were forced into using Dominguez in a key spot Friday in Cleveland, and it didn’t work out. Forced to remove starter Anthony Kay after four innings because of a rain delay, the Sox pieced together a plan that included Dominguez pitching in the seventh inning with a 3-1 lead. He walked two of the three batters he faced, and both came around to score to tie it.</p><p>“We’re talking about delivery, and we’re talking about attacking the strike zone more,” Dominguez said, “attacking the strike zone” being a common refrain among Sox pitchers. “This is the key for me right now: be more aggressive in the strike zone and try to make better pitches.”</p><p>It sounds simple, but manager Will Venable explained why that has been hard for Dominguez, whose 5.5 walks per nine innings also would be the worst of his career.</p><p>“His stuff just moves so much,” Venable said. “We’re trying to harness his stuff and get it into the zone. That’s obviously something we know all our guys are working on. For him, there’s just different considerations, whether it be catcher targeting or where he’s trying to start some of these pitches. Just got to figure out a way to get him in the zone. So that’s what he’s working on, and working hard at it.”</p><p>Dominguez still has 12 saves this season, his most since he had 16 as a rookie with the Phillies in 2018. But 11 came in April and May. After leaning on Dominguez in those months, the Sox have shifted to a bullpen by committee, which has worked more than it hasn’t. And at least until Dominguez finds the strike zone, Venable is sticking with it.</p><p>“We’re going to be consistent with how we’ve approached this,” he said. “Call these guys whatever you want to call them, we’re going to find the best spot for these guys to be successful and do everything we can to find the right pockets of opposing lineups. There’s all kinds of considerations as we try to find a path to the end of these games. So it’s going to look different every single night, like it did before.”</p><p>That has led to seven pitchers earning saves for the Sox, led by Bryan Hudson, Sean Newcomb and Grant Taylor with three each. Taylor and Newcomb earned consecutive saves Saturday and Sunday to help the Sox earn a series split with the Guardians.</p><p>“I have struggled before,” Dominguez said. “I know [those] moments are going to happen, but it’s hard when you’re in those moments. But it’s like I said before: put on your best face, [give] your best effort and try to find a way to help the team win.”</p><p>Dominguez also could give the Sox valuable postseason experience, having pitched for the Blue Jays on their run to the World Series last season. But even then, walks were a problem. He issued 11 free passes with 10 strikeouts in 11 ⅓ postseason innings.</p><p>Fortunately for him, he has felt supported by his teammates.</p><p>“This is a really good clubhouse,” Dominguez said. “We are a unit, everyone. Everybody tries to make you feel good and doesn’t let you put your head down.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Sky shake up starting lineup, crank up defense to beat Mercury
entries.summary: <p>PHOENIX — It's been a stormy start to the week amid a stormy start to the season.</p><p>But the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> weathered both Tuesday, pulling out a 77-66 win over the Mercury behind 16 points from rookie Sydney Taylor and a much improved defensive effort. </p><p>"I think we did a really good job playing off one another, feeding off each other's energy," Taylor said. "They went on their little runs, we went on ours. We took it to the chest, stayed down, we stayed connected, and finished strong."</p><p>The win snapped the Mercury's three-game winning streak. It also came after a starting lineup shakeup that sent point guard Skylar Diggins to the bench and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/07/skylar-diggins-and-tyler-marsh-still-not-aligned-after-benching" >exposed tension between her and coach Tyler Marsh</a>. Diggins ended up a late-scratch, out with a right knee injury that surfaced pregame.</p><p>Even without their second-leading scorer, the Sky (7-14) had more than enough, taking advantage of a depleted Mercury team was turning the ball over left and right. </p><p>The Sky closed the third quarter on an 11-2 run to lead 56-42 behind Taylor's hot shooting and a defense that had been slipping.</p><p>"We're a really great defensive team," Natasha Cloud said. "We started the season like top three, and then we got away from it, but that is our identity and our offense will always come from it."</p><p>Courtney Vandersloot started at point guard in Diggins' place, though she remains on a minutes restriction and sat to open the second half so the team could manage her workload.</p><p>Cloud returned to the starting lineup on the wing and finished with 11 points, six assists, four rebounds and two steals, including a 30-footer that pushed the lead to 20 midway through the fourth.</p><p>Marsh said he liked what he saw from the new look but is still evaluating what will work going forward.</p><p>Cloud said that starting or not, her "job is to show up every single night."</p><p>"The job is to get a win for the Chicago Sky, and that's what I'll do," she said. "So whether it's starting, coming off the bench, guarding a four, guarding the one, whatever I got to do, I'm gonna do it."</p><p>She added: "We're not worried about that outside noise. We're just taking one game at a time. We got a win tonight in Phoenix and we have an LA trip coming next. Just one game at a time, but we're doing it together."</p>

entries.author: Georgia Nicols

entries.title: Noah Schultz struggles again as punchless White Sox fall to Red Sox
entries.summary: <p>Left-hander Noah Schultz had another rough outing in his second start since returning from the injured list.</p><p>Schultz allowed four runs, seven hits and three walks in five innings in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>’ 8-1 loss to the Red Sox at Rate Field. He gave up a solo home run to Andruw Monasterio and a two-run shot to Ceddanne Rafaela in the second, both on sweepers.</p><p>“I felt I had good command, good feel for the cutter,” Schultz said. “But this is a lineup that I wanted to go heavy offspeed. Not being able to land the sweeper or changeup as much as I’d like to [was] definitely frustrating.”</p><p>Schultz, who was on the injured list for just over a month with tendinitis in his right knee, allowed three runs, two hits and four walks in 4 1/3 innings in the White Sox' 6-1 loss to the Orioles on July 1. He also had seven strikeouts. </p><p>In 10 starts this season, Schultz has a 6.00 ERA (32 earned runs in 48 innings) with 29 walks and 43 strikeouts.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/07/chicago-white-sox-seranthony-dominguez-will-venable-bryan-hudson-sean-newcomb-grant-taylor-blue-jays" >White Sox reliever Seranthony Dominguez having ‘a hard moment’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/07/munetaka-murakami-chicago-white-sox-charlotte-knights-rehab-assignment-will-venable-austin-hays-everson-pereira-noah-schultz" >Munetaka Murakami goes 1-for-3 with two strikeouts in first rehab game</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>"A lot of things to work on," he said. "Walks have been pretty high, something that I’m not too happy with. Something I need to clean up for sure with mechanics and finding out my identity as a pitcher with pitch mixes and seeing what to throw most and figuring out different lineups and how to attack them."</p><p>Red Sox lefty Payton Tolle did a great job attacking the White Sox with his fastball. He allowed two hits and one walk in six innings and struck out six.</p><p>"He’s got a really good fastball, and he commanded it well and really beat us in the zone with it," White Sox manager Will Venable said. "Saw a lot of foul balls; just weren’t able to move anything forward. Then he was able to get to the offspeed stuff, as well."</p><p>After Tolle left, the White Sox loaded the bases with no outs in the seventh but scored only once. Kyle Teel drove in the run on a fielder's choice. The Red Sox then turned to right-hander Justin Slaten, who struck out pinch hitter Jacob Gonzalez and Tristan Peters to end the threat.</p><p>Sam Antonacci had three of the White Sox' hits, all against left-handers (lefty Danny Coulombe followed Tolle). He entered the game batting .149 against lefties.<br></p>

entries.title: Woman, 66, shot as nearby car passengers exchange gunfire in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A 66-year-old woman was shot Tuesday night while waiting for a ride in Englewood, according to Chicago police.</p><p>She was standing outside around 10 p.m. in the 800 block of West 59th Street when passengers in two passing vehicles exchanged gunfire, police said. She was struck in the chest and taken to University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition, police said.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said.</p>

entries.title: Chicago Public Media launching community website — chicago.com — in the fall
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Media, owner of the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ, announced plans to launch a website this fall focused on local communities — called chicago.com.</p><p>The site will include Chicago-area information, civic and cultural resources, community-sourced knowledge and opportunities for audience participation, the nonprofit said Wednesday. It will also curate headlines from the Sun-Times, WBEZ and other news sources.</p><p>For independent journalism to “truly service the public, … we should have digital infrastructure that is also steered by public media companies,” Chicago Public Media CEO Melissa Bell said. The news industry “has ceded a lot of distribution to places like Facebook and X, formerly known as Twitter, and I think that has done a disservice to centering civic discourse in a healthy way.”</p><p>She didn’t disclose investments into chicago.com, but said the site is funded by ongoing fundraising by Chicago Public Media.</p><p>The launch will consist of a “minimally viable product”, or a basic website, that will continue to evolve, according to Bell.</p><p>She cited other media outlets around the world as models for chicago.com. They include Village Media in Canada, Front Porch Forum in Vermont, Zetland Media in Denmark and Daily Maverick in South Africa.</p><p>Chicago Public Media will not hire new editorial staff for the site but will enlist current employees, Bell said.</p><p>Last year, the Sun-Times culled <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2025/03/18/chicago-sun-times-lose-20-staff-buyout-offer" >20% of the news staff</a> through buyouts, which included senior editors, high-profile columnists and most of the editorial board. In 2024, Chicago Public Media had layoffs that largely affected WBEZ staff and programming.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure representing unionized employees, said in a statement: “We’re optimistic that this new platform will serve our audiences well and attract new ones. We’re eager to learn more about how our members’ work will be featured while ensuring that union jobs at Chicago Public Media are protected.”</p><p>People are increasingly finding information through social media, online communities, search engines and social media creators, Chicago Public Media said in a news release. Yet many find it difficult to find trusted local information, according to a survey of Chicago residents by the Civic Information Needs Census in partnership with Chicago Public Media.</p><p>Launching chicago.com will help people address that information gap, Chicago Public Media said.</p><p>The website went live on Wednesday, and visitors can sign up for updates and early access, as well as join opportunities to share ideas for the site.</p><p>The Chicago Community Trust, which manages investments and gifts for foundations and family donors, owned the inactive chicago.com domain and gifted it to Chicago Public Media. The Trust didn’t disclose the value of its in-kind gift.</p><p>Michael Ferro, former chairman of Wrapports, which previously owned the Chicago Sun-Times, made a gift in 2017 to The Chicago Community Trust to acquire the chicago.com URL for an undisclosed sum.</p><p>The foundation originally intended to eventually use the domain for the public good in Chicago, Andrea Sáenz, CEO of The Chicago Community Trust, said.</p><p>“The idea that the Chicago Public Media team is developing, and the idea that they brought to us, was really well-aligned with what we hope to do,” she said.</p><p>Chicago.com will eventually be a digital hub serving the city and suburbs by providing news and information and encouraging civic life, Sáenz said.</p><p>The Trust envisions a shared space “where people could come together as Chicagoans, but also still highlight the unique activities and news of each neighborhood and community,” she said.</p><p>Chicago Public Media’s new brand comes at a time when many news organizations are struggling financially. However, Bell said 2026 financial projections indicate Chicago Public Media will be “close to break-even.”</p><p>Chicago Public Media, parent of WBEZ, in 2022 acquired the Sun-Times and converted it from a for-profit to nonprofit status, through a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2022/1/31/22911173/chicago-public-media-sun-times-sale-wbez-parent-donations-donors-philanthropy" >$61 million, five-year pledge</a> from philanthropists and foundations.</p><p>Revenue for the Sun-Times and WBEZ has dropped in recent years, according to tax filings. WBEZ faced a drop in funding when the federal government cut public broadcasting grants, but filled the gap through fundraising.</p><p>Tax filings show Sun-Times revenue fell from $40.4 million in fiscal year 2023 to $31.4 million in fiscal year 2025. The revenue comes mostly from newspaper circulation and secondarily from print and digital advertising.</p><p>WBEZ revenue was $35.6 million in fiscal year 2025, compared with $38.7 million in fiscal year 2023. The money comes mostly from grants and memberships.</p>

entries.title: Girl, 8, fatally struck by lightning during storm in LaSalle County
entries.summary: <p>An 8-year-old girl was fatally struck by lightning in LaSalle County on Friday evening during a storm, officials announced.</p><p>The girl was in the backyard of her home in Serena, Illinois, about 70 miles southwest of Chicago, Friday evening when it happened, the LaSalle County Coroner’s Office said. The coroner's office was called to the emergency room of OSF St. Elizabeth Hospital in Ottawa for the incident. </p><p>An autopsy completed Sunday indicated she died from injuries related to the lightening strike, according to the coroner's office. </p><p>Rain showers and thunderstorms were moving through the area at the time of the incident, according to the National Weather Service. </p><p>"If you're outside during a thunderstorm, your chances for being struck go up significantly," said Zachary Yack, a meteorologist with the weather service. "The old saying goes: when thunder roars, go indoors." </p><p>The incident is under further investigation by the LaSalle County Coroner’s Office and the LaSalle County Sheriff’s office.</p>

entries.title: Looking for coffee at the Obama Presidential Center? The '44 Reserve' blend has 40-year Chicago legacy
entries.summary: <p>Rhonda Stivers always loved coffee. </p><p>As an international flight attendant, the native Chicagoan would frequent coffee shops around the world. And she purchased a bright-red espresso machine, her first, in 1976.</p><p>By 1985, she convinced her then-husband, Greg Stivers, to open Color Me Coffee in Lake View — making them one of the few coffee shops in Chicago to roast beans on-site. That same year, a young Barack Obama first arrived in Chicago.</p><p>Forty years later, the two have become linked. Color Me Coffee was recently named the sole coffee supplier for the newly opened <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/06/02/museum-tower-obama-presidential-center-maligned-signature-building-worthy-consideration" >Obama Presidential Center</a>.</p><p>After a blind taste test that included seven other local roasters, the brand was chosen as the winner in February. The judges included representatives from the Obama Foundation, Bon Appetit magazine and the Chicago Beverage Co.</p><p>The Lower West Side roastery now supplies the presidential center's restaurant, cafe and catering events. Visitors can also purchase their beans at the Cafe inside the center, though they were sold out on Tuesday morning. </p><p>In honor of former President Barack Obama, Stivers and staff created the 44 Reserve, a proprietary blend of Kenyan, Hawaiian and Indonesian beans, symbolizing Obama’s roots. The blend is available at the center and on Color Me Coffee's website.</p><p>Stivers isn’t sure if the Obamas have tasted Color Me Coffee yet.</p><p>“We do know they have espresso machines in their entries.title: Dear Abby: Computer repair leads to upsetting discovery
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been married to my wife for three years. She asked me to fix her old computer. As I was doing that, I saw emails from her ex, "Doug," dated a few months before our wedding. They started with the usual greetings, then proceeded to steamy back-and-forth emails.</p><p>They set up a time to talk, and Doug suggested they use FaceTime. It appears they had several interactions on FaceTime. In his emails afterward (she told him never to text), he described his sexual feelings and how great her body looked and details about what he was going to do to her. She played right back with him. This went on for about a month and a half. When she cut it off, he complained, but she never got back to him.</p><p>Doug emailed her several times after the last interaction and asked why she had stopped, adding that he was giving up after receiving no response. I noted his number was also blocked on her phone. He lives in another country, so I know they didn't physically get together. We have a good marriage, but this is killing me. What should I do? — <i>BETRAYED IN NEW YORK</i></p><p><b>DEAR BETRAYED:</b> What you should do is tell your wife you found her correspondence with Doug and how it made you feel. She realized she was making a mistake and ended her inappropriate conversations with Doug before she married you. I presume she has been faithful ever since. Feeling as you do, you may need the help of a licensed marriage counselor to put this matter to rest. Please don't wait.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband throws a fit over every minor inconvenience, from the trash can being knocked over to the screen door being in his way. He starts yelling and cursing and slamming doors. I don't understand it. When things like this happen to other people, they simply pick up the mess or move the object and go about their day.</p><p>I try to help and move stuff around to avoid his fits, but they are inevitable, it seems. I cannot handle the negativity over something so trivial. Our neighbors can hear him, and I'd feel embarrassed, if I were him, to be heard cursing like a child having a tantrum.</p><p>How would you advise I handle this situation? I am at my wits' end. I feel as though I will have to live with the yelling and anger forever. — <i>IN THE LINE OF FIRE</i></p><p><b>DEAR IN THE LINE:</b> Could there be some other stressors in your husband's life that have caused him to have such a short fuse? When folks are troubled about something they can't control, they sometimes blame their frustration on the nearest person or object. It's called "displacement."</p><p>I hope you realize that his inability to control his temper (and his mouth) is no reflection on you, and that it is not up to you to handle it. If you manage to catch him when he's rational, ask if anything else might be bothering him, and then be prepared to listen. If he realizes what's causing this, it might make him better able to cope.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For everything you need to know about wedding planning, order "How to Have a Lovely Wedding." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Wedding Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: CPS parents are still waiting for state to properly fund schools
entries.summary: <p>As a father of three Chicago Public Schools students, I was encouraged to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/06/25/cps-says-it-wont-cut-instructional-time-or-safe-passage-program-in-upcoming-budget" target="_blank" >read</a> that CPS will not reduce instructional time or eliminate Safe Passage as it works to close a $732 million budget gap. Those are the right priorities.</p><p>But this moment should also serve as a wake-up call.</p><p>Every summer, parents are forced to wonder what programs, staff or services will be on the chopping block. Schools cannot thrive when they spend months planning around financial uncertainty instead of focusing on teaching and learning.</p><p>The real issue is not whether CPS can protect instructional time this year — it's whether Illinois is willing to fully invest in the students it serves. According to the state's own Evidence-Based Funding formula, CPS still receives only <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/media/community-updates/2026/may/budget-process/" target="_blank" >about 73% of the funding</a> needed to provide an adequate education. That leaves our children competing for resources they should already have.</p><p>Parents, educators, community, business and elected leaders should all be working toward the same goal: giving every child the opportunity to succeed. That means finding sustainable solutions that protect classrooms, support educators and provide the stable funding our students deserve — not annual budget crises that pit one essential service against another.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker recently <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FEtjAIHhSOA" target="_blank" >said</a>, "Our kids deserve every day of education that parents demand." </p><p>I couldn't agree more. </p><p>Now is the time for the governor and the Illinois General Assembly to convene a special session and identify additional investments in public education, including increasing evidence-based funding. Our children deserve a funding system that matches our state's commitment to them.</p><p>Chicago's students should not have to wonder each year whether their education will become another budget negotiation. They deserve certainty, opportunity and leaders who will work together to make that possible.</p><p><i>Claiborne Wade, co-chair, Austin Community Action Council, and chairman, Kids First Chicago's Equitable Funding Task Force</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b10000" name="module-b10000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Stalling makes Social Security fixes harder</h3><p>Each year, the Social Security Trustees Report produces the same bad debate. One side says Social Security is going bankrupt. The other says there's nothing to worry about.</p><p>Both are wrong.</p><p>The 2026 <a class="Link" href="https://www.ssa.gov/oact/trsum/" target="_blank" >report</a> doesn't say Social Security is disappearing. It says the system is still paying benefits, but the cost of fixing it is getting larger the longer Congress waits.</p><p>The combined trust funds are still projected to be depleted in 2034. If that happens, incoming payroll taxes would still cover about 83% of scheduled benefits. That is not bankruptcy. It's also not stability.</p><p>The more important warning is that the program’s 75-year actuarial deficit grew from 3.82% of taxable payroll last year to 4.42% this year. The deadline did not move, but the repair bill got 16% bigger.</p><p>As a registered Social Security analyst, I sit across from families deciding when to claim benefits. Many ask whether they should claim early because they fear the system will collapse. That fear often leads to poor planning.</p><p>For many retirees, the greater risk is not that Social Security vanishes but living into their 80s or 90s after claiming at 62 and accepting a smaller check for life.</p><p>In 1983, lawmakers made <a class="Link" href="https://www.ssa.gov/history/1983amend.html" target="_blank" >changes to Social Security</a> that bought decades of stability. But waiting made the politics harder then and waiting is making the math harder now.</p><p>There's no mystery about the possible fixes: raise more revenue, adjust future benefits, change the wage cap, raise the retirement age or combine several tools. Every option makes someone unhappy, which is why lawmakers delay. But arithmetic does not wait for political courage.</p><p>Social Security is not bankrupt, but delay is expensive. Retirees should not let fear drive personal claiming decisions. Congress should not let fear drive inaction.</p><p>The warning light is on. The car is still running. But the longer Congress drives past the repair shop, the bigger the bill becomes.</p><p><i>Ray R. Harris, founder and president, Social Security Claiming Experts</i></p><h3>Superb Snelling </h3><p>Supt. Larry Snelling last week announced <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/07/01/larry-snelling-chicago-superintendent-police-retire" >his retirement effective July 15</a> after three years of heading up the Chicago Police Department. </p><p>Leadership starts at the top, and Supt. Snelling, in my opinion, and the majority of Chicago's rank-and-file cops agree: He was one of the best. </p><p>There is an expression often said about popular top cops — “he was a cop's cop.” Supt. Snelling indeed fits that mold, but he also has been a people’s cop. If I listed all the great qualities of a leader, he would undoubtedly check all the boxes. </p><p>Leadership is not about control — it’s about courage when control is lost. Supt. Snelling's leadership and constant presence during the 2024 Democratic National Convention drew worldwide praise. </p><p>When the federal ICE raids last year turned Chicago's streets into chaotic confusion, his steady hand prevented even more violence and confusion. Chicago was fortunate to have such a man. Supt. Snelling is made of the right stuff.</p><p><i>Bob Angone, retired Chicago Police lieutenant, Austin, Texas</i></p><h3>Give homeowners a break on lead pipe replacement</h3><p>I read recently in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/06/30/chicago-has-most-lead-pipes-why-is-it-so-expensive-to-replace-them" target="_blank" >Sun-Times</a> that the city can charge a few thousand dollars for permits for a homeowner to replace a lead water service line. That’s a good way to keep lead pipes in service. If the city is serious about replacing lead pipes, it should waive all permit fees to replace lead pipes.</p><p><i>Tom Vega-Byrnes, Beverly</i></p><h3>He probably flunked history </h3><p>President Donald Trump sometimes gets it wrong. A few days ago, he called three winners of Democratic congressional primaries in New York City <a class="Link" href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/26/after-progressive-us-primary-wins-trump-takes-aim-at-godless-communists" target="_blank" >“communists.” </a>They are not. </p><p>Last year, after the election of Zohran Mamdani as mayor of New York, he said: <a class="Link" href="https://www.foxnews.com/media/trump-calls-out-nyc-mayors-very-angry-acceptance-speech-after-recent-election-victory" target="_blank" >“For a thousand years communism has not worked.”</a> More than a little off target since the foundational piece on communism, <a class="Link" href="https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-21/marx-publishes-manifesto" target="_blank" >“The Communist Manifesto”</a> by Karl Marx (with the assistance of Friedrich Engels), was published in 1848. </p><p>Given that the president has a less-than-solid grasp of history, maybe he thinks that Karl Marx had brothers named Groucho, Chico and Harpo.</p><p><i>Gerald Weisberg, M.D., Lake View</i></p><h3></h3>

entries.title: Obama Presidential Center programming comes into focus, starting with 'La Borinqueña' superhero workshop
entries.summary: <p>The superhero of the moment isn’t Superman or Batman. Nor was she created by legacy studios like Marvel or DC Comics.</p><p>“La Borinqueña,” created by Edgardo Miranda-Rodriguez, an independent writer, graphic novelist and philanthropist based in Brooklyn, has crossed over with some of DC Comics’ iconic characters. entries.title: ‘Shell-shocked’ Chicago scientists raise alarm about federal overhaul of research grant funding
entries.summary: <p>After working for years in the pharmaceutical industry, Joseph Dominguez enjoyed the freedom to take on scientific research he found in an academic institution that had no commercial ties.</p><p>Dominguez finished his Ph.D. earlier this year after studying the role of innate immune cells in early ovarian cancer, which was funded through a federal grant for the past two years. He considered continuing in academia, but will likely return to the private sector in part because of greater scrutiny from the government over funding for research, particularly women’s health, which has been in the crosshairs of the Trump administration as “DEI-focused.”</p><p>“It’s just health sciences — women’s health, men’s health — it’s all very critical,” Dominguez said. “They want to ban all DEI wording, ‘gender ideology.’ There have been professors who have been working on women’s health and ovarian cancer who have had their funding taken. I can very much see scenarios where this will take away our funding.”</p><p>Dominguez, along with other researchers in Chicago, are mobilizing their peers to submit public comments ahead of a proposed rule they say would significantly change the country’s approach to funding science innovation and research. The Office of <a class="Link" href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/29/2026-10817/regulation-for-federal-financial-assistance" target="_blank" ><u>Management and Budget</u></a> is proposing a rule to<b> </b>overhaul guidance for federal financial assistance, which includes grants issued by the National Institutes of Health, and turn it into a rule. It would go into effect as soon as Oct. 1.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1d0000" name="module-1d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>What the Trump administration is proposing</b><br><br>The proposed “<a class="Link" href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/29/2026-10817/regulation-for-federal-financial-assistance" target="_blank" ><u>Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance</u></a>” rule will make several changes to how the federal government manages funding for scientific research and other fields. Here’s how the process would be impacted, according to experts and Chicago-based researchers.<br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-14a402d1-7a3e-11f1-992d-eb712c3be2a4"><li><b>Mid-stream grant cancellations:</b> Grants could be terminated or suspended with little due process, said Joanne Padrón Carney with the American Association for the Advancement of Science. The termination does not have to include evidence of noncompliance or fraud. Causes for a termination include that a project no longer aligns with “Federal agency priorities, or the national interest.”</li><li><b>Inserting political appointees:</b> Senior appointees would get a formal role in the grant review process rather than leaving it up to a peer review process, as was the practice. </li><li><b>Limits to international research:</b> American scientists say it’s not uncommon to work with international researchers, but the proposed rule would restrict collaborations. For example, one part says funds can’t go to “foreign entities” unless there’s an authorized statute or a “compelling reason.” </li><li><b>Anti-American denials: </b>The proposed rule points to broad terms that studies must help the country restore “gold standard science” and that the work can’t be deemed “anti-American.” Experts say the rule would allow funding denials if the institution where a researcher works is looked at as promoting “anti-American values.” </li></ul></div> </div><p>More than 82,000 people so far have submitted public comments, including at least three dozen that reference Chicago. The comment period ends July 13.</p><p>In its summary of the rule, the Office of Management and Budget says it is proposing the changes to improve “transparency, accountability and oversight” of funds. In addition, the government says it is seeking ways to reduce the misuse and waste of tax dollars.</p><p>But researchers in Chicago say the proposed rule would upend the scientific research enterprise that has been in place since World War II and has long been seen as the world’s most robust. The new rule would give political appointees, rather than scientists, formal say over what research gets funded. It would also allow for grants to be terminated mid-stream if they're not aligned with the executive branch’s priorities, and studies deemed “anti-American” would not be approved, among other changes.</p><p>Already, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/05/25/northwestern-uic-medical-researchers-diabetes-hiv-trump-funding-budget-cuts" target="_blank" ><u>researchers have faced grant denials or delays</u></a> as the Trump administration has made it increasingly difficult to secure federal funding over the last 18 months. Some of those delays are because political appointees are already reviewing research grants, said Joanne Padrón Carney, the chief government relations officer for the D.C.-based American Association for the Advancement of Science.</p><p>“This proposed rule would kind of set in stone some of the activities that we have already been seeing in the past year and a half and make it very difficult to change,” Padrón Carney said.</p><p>The rule would turn what was previously guidance that federal agencies could modify into federal regulation, she said.</p><p>“It kind of codifies it, to have like a force of law across all in the entire federal government,” she said. “This impacts all sectors of society, not just the research community.”</p><h2>Risking abrupt grant terminations</h2><p>Dr. Ravi Kalhan, a Chicago-based pulmonary doctor and professor at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, might have thought twice about his career choice two decades ago if he had known how precarious federal funding would become.</p><p>Kalhan submitted a public comment ahead of the proposed rule implementation. He is particularly worried about language in the proposal that says a grant could be terminated if it “is not effective at achieving program goals or Federal agency priorities, or that an agency otherwise determines is no longer in the Federal Government’s interest.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Huh/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kalhan is currently leading federally funded research into lung health. It includes establishing a cohort of healthy 25- to 35-year-olds and studying them long-term to see what factors, such as exposure, lifestyle or diet, contribute to developing chronic lung disease later in life.</p><p>“You can’t study the prevention of diseases that take a lifetime to develop if the research program can get canceled in six months or a year,” Kalhan said.</p><p>For now, Kalhan doesn’t think his research is at risk because the current administration has indicated it wants to prevent chronic disease.</p><p>“It seems like a waste to sort of invest all this time and energy in forming a cohort, for example, that we plan to follow for a long time and then deciding because it’s no longer a priority to study a condition or a factor in a condition that we are going to cancel that program,” Kalhan said. “... Terminating it before answers come about seems equally wasteful to me.”</p><h2>Changes to peer review process</h2><p>The new rule would add a political appointee’s opinion on the merits of a proposal into a process that has long been left to scientists. Chicago-based researcher Timothy Koh says that will dramatically change the process and curtail progress in scientific research.</p><p>Now, researchers submit a proposal to be funded for three to five years, and it typically undergoes review by a panel of experts in that field that evaluate the science and if it could advance the field, Koh said.</p><p>The proposed rule calls for a senior appointee, named by the U.S. president, to review discretionary grants to ensure they are consistent with agency priorities and the national interest.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> And this would just throw all that away.”</p><p>Carole LaBonne, a stem cell biologist and developmental biologist, said based on her experience with grants she interprets the proposal as allowing the appointee to weigh in before the funds are issued. LaBonne said she and her peers worry that could mean a proposal could be denied if the appointee doesn’t agree with the field of study or because of the person’s affiliations or location.</p><p>The proposed rule also makes references to so-called “gold standard science,” but doesn’t define it, raising questions about what kind of research will get denied.</p><p>“They’ve inserted all these ways that they can terminate grants either to particular areas of research, particular investigators or particular universities, with no ability to push back on that in the [same] way that has been happening in the last year and a half,” said LaBonne, who is a professor at Northwestern University.</p><h2>‘Shell-shocked’ community</h2><p>The changes to funding that have already taken place have caused so much stress that some researchers are taking anxiety medications for the first time, LaBonne said.</p><p>“Every scientist that I know at every institution across every state is pretty much shell-shocked right now,” LaBonne said. “We don’t view what we do as a job, it’s who we are. In some sense it’s your identity that is being attacked.”</p><p>There are efforts to push back, said Dr. Georges Benjamin, chief executive officer for the American Public Health Association. His organization has challenged the Trump administration’s cuts to research grants in court, including those that were deemed to be part of diversity, equity and inclusion efforts.</p><p>“One of the reasons we’ve been so far successful is that they didn’t follow the rules,” Benjamin said, referring to one court ruling that initially determined NIH had improperly ended grants related to diversity efforts, though litigation continues. “So now what they’re trying to do with this OMB rule is put in place all the illegal practices that they’ve been following and try to basically … do what they’ve been doing by basically saying, ‘Yeah, we have the right to do this through the regulatory process.’”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: One of Mayor Brandon Johnson's most ardent City Council adversaries won't seek reelection in 2027
entries.summary: <p>Ald. Marty Quinn (13th), who learned the game of Chicago politics at the feet of now-convicted former Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan (D-Chicago), is calling it a career after 15 years in the City Council.</p><p>Quinn, 51, <a class="Link" href="<iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_ec1fad9d-6972-4ca8-a782-47ec7e1fa3d4&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml ”style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe>" target="_blank" >told the Sun-Times</a> that he has decided not to seek reelection in 2027.</p><p>After 4,100 conversations in the last four years alone in the living rooms and at the front doors of his Southwest Side constituents, Quinn said he “left it all on the field” and no longer has the energy required to “manage from the front lines.” He said he cannot risk giving the demanding job less than it demands.</p><p>“It’s not easy, and it’s not predictable. A couple of weeks ago, we had a tornado reported through Clearing. I was out with the ward superintendent until 2 a.m. 'cause you can’t manage what you don’t know. A year ago this time, we dealt with over 1,200 basement floodings,” he said.</p><p>“You stop everything, including your personal life… I’m glued to every forecast in the winter looking for the snowflakes to come because I’m on the job," Quinn said. "At this point in my life, it’s time for me to move along… It’s just my time. I’m just ready.”</p><p>Four years ago, a record dozen members of the City Council chose political retirement over the battle for reelection.</p><p>This time around, Quinn is the first veteran alderperson to make that life-changing decision.</p><p>Quinn was part of a renegade bloc of moderate Democrats who rejected Mayor Brandon Johnson’s corporate head tax and passed an alternative city budget with major elements Johnson opposes.</p><p>Quinn's departure will deny that rebel group one of its most reliable votes and best political tacticians.</p><p>Their loss is Mayor Brandon Johnson’s gain.</p><p>Quinn has gone toe-to-toe with the mayor on everything from the now-vetoed Chicago ban on hemp-derived products to the failed quest for a new Southwest Side police station and the successful effort to force Johnson to settle for a weaker version of the long-stalled granny flat ordinance.</p><p>Although he has clashed repeatedly with Johnson, Quinn is also a political pragmatist.</p><p>He predicted that Johnson would be a shoo-in to make the mayoral runoff and could overcome his low-30s public approval rating to win a second term on the strength of "five basic supporter groups.” </p><p>They are the Chicago Teachers Union, Democratic Socialists of America, African-American voters over 50, voters 18 to 25 years old who “never show up on polls" but showed up to blindside Paul Vallas in 2023, and the 622,000 renters whom Johnson is “trying to get his arms around” with his protecting renters ordinance.</p><p>“You put those folks together, there’s room for him to grow," Quinn said. "I wouldn’t rule the CTU out. I wouldn’t rule the Democratic Socialists of America out. I wouldn’t do that. We saw what happened in New York a couple weeks ago."</p><p>For years, Quinn served as one of the most trusted political lieutenants in Madigan’s vaunted and once-impenetrable 13th Ward Regular Democratic Organization.</p><p>Madigan’s political downfall began with a “Me Too” scandal involving Quinn’s brother Kevin.</p><p>Kevin Quinn’s firing for sexual harassment in 2018 triggered a trail of hidden payments that federal prosecutors used to expose a culture of corruption in Madigan’s inner circle.</p><p>Marty Quinn was accused of playing a pivotal go-between role between his own brother and political consultant Alaina Hampton, who accused Kevin Quinn of stalking her with a series of harassing text messages.</p><p>Marty Quinn has no regrets about his own conduct.</p><p>“I did everything Alaina asked me to do. The minute I found out about the interaction, I called Kevin into the office and said, 'You make one more text message to her, you will be fired on the spot,'” the retiring alderperson said.</p><p>“It was a very difficult time professionally and personally in my life… A very public situation that wasn’t an easy time for our family. Not an easy thing to go through.”</p><p>Madigan was sentenced to 7.5 years in prison after choosing to take the stand in his own defense and lying during that testimony, according to the judge.</p><p>Quinn said he has talked to his 83-year-old mentor three times while in prison.</p><p>“I would just ask him how he’s doing and he’d say, 'I’m doing okay.’ And then, it’s on to whatever is that is the issue at hand,” the alderperson said.</p><p>“The last conversation was about affordable housing. That warmed my heart because those are the conversations we would have [before]. Those are the kinds of interactions that I love having with Speaker Madigan because he’s so well-read.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-ca0000" name="html-embed-module-ca0000"></a><iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_ec1fad9d-6972-4ca8-a782-47ec7e1fa3d4&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml "style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Lung transplants extend lives of sickest cancer patients better than standard treatment: study
entries.summary: <p>Patients with advanced lung cancer are far more likely to survive if they receive a lung transplant compared to patients who received a standard cancer treatment, a landmark study from Northwestern Medicine found. </p><p>The medical community has long considered it too risky to transplant lungs into patients with advanced cancer because of the potential risk for cancer cells to spread to the new lungs. </p><p>But the new study, published Wednesday in the Journal of the American Medical Association, challenges that notion, said Dr. Ankit Bharat, Northwestern's chief of thoracic surgery and a co-author of the study. </p><p>Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the U.S. It's also the most common part of the body for other types of cancers to spread to, Bharat said. </p><p>The study included 404 adults with end-stage pulmonary disease, including 98 patients with stage four lung cancer. Of that group, 17 received a lung transplant and 89 were treated with standard cancer treatments from September 2021 through June 2025. The patients in the study only received a lung transplant if the cancer was isolated to their lungs, had caused significant damage to their lungs and if they had exhausted all other standard treatments, like immunotherapy and chemotherapy.</p><p>During the nearly four-year study period, every transplant patient was alive after a year, while less than half of patients treated with medical therapy alone were alive after a year.</p><p>"Those patients were not only dying from cancer, but they can’t breathe. They're likely on a ventilator, and they basically had no life left," Bharat said.</p><p>The lung transplant also turned the patients' conditions around. One of Bharat's patients was about to withdraw care when they offered the lung transplant. He survived.</p><p>"That's one of the most profound aspects of this study is how patients benefited from it," Bharat said. "They were at the end of their lives and had no other hope, no other treatment options. Then we were able to extend their life and give them a higher quality of life, too."</p><p>Bharat told the Sun-Times the idea for the study came while he and his colleagues were treating patients hospitalized with COVID-19 early on in the pandemic. </p><p>The experience made Bharat wonder if that approach can be replicated with patients suffering from advanced lung cancer that was isolated in the lungs. </p><p>"We were the first in the nation to understand how COVID was killing people and destroying the framework of the lungs," Bharat said. "Our observation from that was that the only way to save these patients was to replace these lungs, which was very controversial at the time because these were really sick patients."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/05/11/chicago-health-lung-cancer-northwestern-medicine-mothers-day-mom-twins-transplant" >Mother of twins upends her life for double lung transplant in Chicago after failed cancer treatments</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Family of 2 siblings killed in Lake Geneva boat accident raise money to support charity in their memory
entries.summary: <p>Relatives of two Chicago-area siblings who were 'best friends' and who were killed when a boat capsized in Lake Geneva in Wisconsin Friday are raising money to donate to charity in their memory. </p><p>The children, identified by family as 6-year-old Caleb Oswald and 7-year-old Abigail Oswald were two of three children killed when the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/06/lake-geneva-boat-capsize-wheaton-batavia" target="_blank" >boat capsized</a> Friday afternoon as a severe storm system swept across Walworth County with peak winds between 90 and 100 mph. The third child, who was 10 years old, hasn’t yet been identified. </p><p>As of Wednesday morning, over $15,000 had been raised, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/charity-fund-for-caleb-abigail-oswald?attribution_id=sl:1453b916-20e9-48e0-a381-9ee303e5a2c0&lang=en_US&ts=1783513089&utm_campaign=fp_sharesheet&utm_content=amp20_t1&utm_medium=customer&utm_source=copy_link" target="_blank" >GoFundMe</a>. The funds will be given to a children's charity in Caleb and Abigail's memory. </p><p>"While our hearts are broken beyond words, we want their legacy to be one of hope, compassion, and helping others," the family said in a post attached to the fundraiser. </p><p>Caleb and Abigail's family described the siblings as "best friends" who were "deeply loved by their family, friends, teachers, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing them."</p><p>"They filled our home with laughter, music, hugs, and endless love," the children's parents wrote. </p><p>Caleb was passionate about trucks, music and Chick-fil-A — he often spoke of how he'd work at the food chain when he was older. </p><p>He'd ask Alexa to play his favorite songs and "dance and sing with pure happiness" whenever the music started, according to the fundraiser post. </p><p>"Caleb found happiness in the simple things, and his laughter and excitement were contagious," his parents wrote.</p><p>Abigail loved swimming and dancing and "had the quickest wit of anyone her family knew."</p><p>"She always had a funny comment or joke ready and could make everyone around her laugh," her family said in the fundraiser. "She had a huge heart for others and dreamed of becoming a teacher one day because she wanted to help children learn and grow. She was kind, loving, and wise beyond her years."<br></p>

entries.title: Mayor Brandon Johnson taps new public health commissioner
entries.summary: <p>Dr. Garth Walker, an executive at Rush Health and an emergency department physician, has been appointed Chicago’s next public health commissioner.</p><p>“I’ve spent my career committed to centering a public health approach that addresses the social and economic conditions that shape people’s health and wellbeing,” Walker said in a statement Wednesday announcing his appointment. “As someone who grew up in Chicago, it’s an honor to serve as Commissioner of the Chicago Department of Public Health and support the Mayor’s vision for a healthier Chicago.”</p><p>Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson appointed Walker, but City Council members must approve his new role. He would replace Dr. Olusimbo Ige, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/22/ige-resigns-commissioner-public-health-johnson-arwady" target="_blank" ><u>resigned in May</u></a> after about two and half years on the job.</p><p>As commissioner, Walker would be charged with improving the health of Chicago, one of the most segregated cities in the U.S., with a <a class="Link" href="https://chicagohealthatlas.org/indicators/VRLE?tab=table" target="_blank" ><u>nearly 20-year life expectancy gap</u></a> between neighborhoods. At one point, the so-called death gap<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/chicagos-death-gap" target="_blank" ><u> was the largest</u></a> of any big city in America. The Chicago health department oversees everything from inspecting restaurants to managing disease outbreaks.</p><p>“Dr. Garth Walker has dedicated his career to ensuring every Chicagoan has the opportunity to live a healthy life, regardless of the neighborhood they call home,” Johnson said in the statement. “From leading public health efforts during the COVID-19 pandemic to advancing innovative models of care and addressing the root causes of health disparities, Dr. Walker has demonstrated the leadership and commitment our city needs.”</p><p>Walker is currently the chief medical officer at Rush Health on the Near West Side, which is part of one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the region. He previously was deputy director of the Illinois Department of Public Health during the COVID-19 pandemic. As a White House Fellow with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services during the administration of President Joe Biden, he helped create advisory reports on public health challenges, such as youth mental health and physician burnout.</p><p>Walker also is a scholar. His research focuses on conditions that contribute to a person’s physical and mental health, such as access to a job and stable housing or violence in their community. He’s also studied firearm injury prevention and health care communication.</p><p>Walker grew up in Hyde Park on the South Side, attended Chicago public schools and is on the boards of the Polk Bros. Foundation, Thresholds, and the Chicago Urban League.</p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch is a senior reporter covering public health for WBEZ.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/22/ige-resigns-commissioner-public-health-johnson-arwady" >Dr. Olusimbo Ige out as Chicago health chief</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/chicagos-death-gap" >Chicago’s Death Gap</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
